passage: The "hygiene hypothesis" is often told as a simple warning. Modern homes are so clean that children meet few germs. As a result, their immune systems never learn properly, and allergies follow. Most immune scientists no longer accept that version. The rise in allergies does not match up well with fewer common childhood illnesses, such as colds and flu. Instead, it matches up with less contact with certain ancient, mostly harmless microbes. These "old friends" evolved alongside humans and help tune the immune system. In this newer view, a childhood full of colds gives little protection, while contact with the right microbes from the environment does.

options.F2P1-Q1-D: The "old friend" microbes were far more common in human homes thousands of years ago than in homes today.

In the spring of 1903 the harbor commission of Alder Cove, a fishing port of nine hundred people, met to settle a question it had deferred for six years. Hollis Vane, the engineer the town had hired the previous autumn, laid his plan before the seven commissioners: to cut a second entrance through the sand spit at Low Point, so that vessels need not beat around the shoal in a southerly wind. His estimate was fourteen thousand dollars, more than Alder Cove had ever borrowed at one time. When the meeting opened, the standing motion was the merchant Amos Kerr's, to do the work in stages over ten years and borrow nothing. Two commissioners, Pell and Danforth, had said nothing at all.

What moved them was neither Vane's drawings nor his figures. A letter came from an Army engineer at the district office, undertaking to match, dollar for dollar, whatever Alder Cove itself spent on the cut. Fourteen thousand dollars had suddenly become seven, and Pell and Danforth voted with Vane that evening.

Kerr's answer was not that the work was useless. It was that the district office had given two other towns the same undertaking within his memory and had honored it in neither of them. He lost, five to two, and the town borrowed in June.

The town dug its own half of the cut in 1904 and stopped. The federal money arrived in 1912 and came to less than a third of the sum promised. The entrance was opened to nine feet and never to the fifteen Vane had drawn; vessels used it in fair weather and avoided it in foul. Whether it would have answered at full depth cannot be said. Vane left in 1908 for a larger post, and the minute book gives the whole business one line.

For sixty years the only way across the Kettle River at Harlow Bend was Josiah Pike's flat-bottomed ferry, which took two wagons at a time and stopped altogether whenever the water ran high. In the spring of 1883 the town council met in the schoolhouse to consider a bridge. The clerk, Ada Renwick, kept a minute book that the county archive still holds, and her cramped hand preserves that evening better than any newspaper of the district did.

Renwick's minutes turn on one document alone. A petition from the farmers upriver came to the schoolhouse that evening carrying forty-one names, and Chairman Elias Fenn read every name aloud before anyone spoke. Nothing else came before the council: no surveyor had yet sounded the riverbed, the post office sent no word about the mail route, no court order reached the town, and the river never left its banks that year.

Cordelia Vane, a grain merchant, paid the whole cost from her own funds and took charge of the accounts herself until the last plank was laid. The town treasury gave nothing, the county offered nothing, the mills paid nothing, and no toll was ever taken from anyone who crossed. Fenn waited three weeks for the estimates to arrive before he would allow a vote, and the council then decided the question itself, unforced.

The bridge opened in 1885 and stands yet, square and sound. The old ferry was sold downriver that autumn and worked another twenty years at a landing near the county line. But the grain trade the petitioners had promised turned north to a new railway within two seasons, and the crossing has carried less every year since it opened. The work was carefully done and carefully paid for. It was simply not needed, and I cannot read the minutes without regret.

The figure printed on every ticket is four hours, and she means it. That alone should warn the people who bring children to Teodora Ruiz. These plays are not for children; they are made for grown people, and they hold them. What else is said of her is accurate. The cycle's form is an old village tradition she revived, and her manner changed during her study abroad. She cuts every puppet herself, and no performance of hers was ever recorded.

Slowness is the method. One scene is held motionless for eleven minutes, and that stillness is its whole power; quicken it and nothing remains. The rest is negotiable. A narrator talks throughout and the plays are none the worse. The puppeteers stay hidden behind the screen and nothing is lost. The shapes are sanded smooth as coins, which costs nothing, and the lamp stays fixed in its bracket where no one misses its moving.

It runs an hour too long, which I concede; but the charge that the cycle is cold is false, and I answer it here. It is thick with feeling and never merely clever. I would not call it faultless even now, and it is no falling-off from her early plays either. I said on opening night what I say now and take back nothing. The younger puppeteers in her manner interest me because the manner they work in is one she abandoned years ago. They have understood her no better than her admirers, though they have taken more from her than her mannerisms. Nothing of theirs stands above the work it came from, and no notice will drive them off, since their halls are full.

There is a minute I could quote at length; I leave it alone. I make no prediction about which of her works will survive. I offer no theory of why a crowd is fooled, and advice to other critics I keep out of these columns. The room instead: nobody left, nobody coughed, and they filed out without applauding.

Renna Okoye had watched raccoons along the Ochlockonee for eleven years before she built the box. It was a cube of clear acrylic, forty centimetres on a side, with a single grape resting on the floor where any animal could see the fruit and none could reach it. The lid screwed down onto the body of the box on a coarse thread, and the grip that turned it was a knurled dial the size of a jar lid. Nothing about the box could be lifted or pulled; the dial had to go counterclockwise, three full turns, before the lid would come free.

Okoye set the box at the edge of the clearing one evening in March, backed into a canvas blind, and started the infrared camera. The young male the station called Tilt arrived at 9:14. He circled the box twice, put his forepaws on the lid, and then went to work. He worked the dial for nineteen minutes, mostly clockwise, tightening it. When a paw finally slipped the other way and the lid rose a millimetre, he kept turning in that direction, twenty-odd small strokes, until the lid lifted off.

A single solved box proves very little, and Okoye knew the objection she would hear. Anyone could say he had simply followed the smell of the grape to the seam and worried at whatever his paws found there. So Okoye ran the box empty for three nights with crushed grape rubbed along the bottom edge instead. Tilt went to the dial each time and ignored the scented seam.

Okoye takes the empty-box nights as evidence that Tilt was aiming at the fastening rather than at the odour, while insisting that everything she has is one raccoon's habits. She has ordered eleven more boxes and wants twelve animals tested before she writes a word.

The summer I turned fifteen my parents sent me to Kettle Cove to work for my great-aunt Sabine, who had grown oysters on a leased stretch of tidal flat there since before I was born. She met the bus without smiling and said that the working day began at low water. My work, from June to September, was the tally book: I wrote down the count of every rack on the flat, morning and evening. She did not put me to grading the young stock at the sorting board, or to mending and re-tarring the wire trays, or to rowing the skiff and reading the tide tables; those she kept for herself.

At low tide the flat was a grey field ribbed with racks. The red buoy at the mouth of the channel had been set there by her brother, and she painted it every spring so that the memory of him would stay in plain view. It was not a boundary marker, not a tide signal, and not a warning to strangers about the shoal; it was her brother, kept as near as she could keep him. Twice a week a truck came for the crates.

The word she used for what she wanted from me was check, and she asked for one every morning: the slow look over every tray in turn, one rack at a time. She did not mean a hairline split in a shell, or a written order for money owed, or anything that held the animals back from growing. I learned to answer her in a single word.

She took the largest orders the market offered, lifted racks whenever they were ready, and worked the far flat across the channel like any other ground; the one thing she refused was to let a hand she had not trained herself set foot on the flat. I asked her once whether that refusal had cost her anything, and she said it had. I respected her hands and thought her wrong about the flat, and both of those are still true. She never struck me as comic, I was never a cool observer keeping my distance, and my regard for her was never the unreserved kind.

For six summers, Ivar Solberg and Dana Whitfield studied a single unattended vegetable stand on a county road in northern Vermont. The stand belonged to the Trask family, who set out crates of produce each morning, posted a price list, and left a locked steel box for payment. No one watched the road. Solberg and Whitfield wanted to know what people do when the only thing holding up a price is the price itself.

Their method was deliberately dull. Each evening an assistant weighed what remained, counted the money, and computed a compliance rate: money received divided by money owed. Across the first two summers that rate sat between 61 and 64 percent and barely moved from one day of the week to the next. Two customers in five paid nothing at all; a much smaller group paid above the list price, apparently covering for the rest.

In the third summer the researchers changed one thing. They mounted a small mirror on the post above the cash box, angled so that anyone reaching for the slot met their own face for a moment. Whitfield's reasoning was that people behave differently when reminded of being watched, even when the watcher is themselves.

The season that followed is the part of the study people cite. Compliance in the hours before noon, when the mirror caught the light, averaged 81 percent; in the shaded afternoon it averaged 62 percent. The two figures were reported side by side rather than folded into a season average, and the gap between them is the finding.

Solberg is cautious about what a number like that can carry. The stand sits on one road in one county, and the drivers who stop there are not a random sample of anyone; a stand outside a city, he notes, might behave nothing like it. The result registered with the Trask family long before it reached any table of his; they had been saying for years that mornings paid better than afternoons, and Solberg allows that the study mostly caught up with what the people running the stand already knew.

Dumitra put her accordion into my hands at the fair, and the whole yard waited, and I did not play. Everybody there still has a reason for it: that my hand was cut; that I wanted Dumitra to play; that the D reed was dead; that I never knew their tune; that I had promised my aunt. Only one of them is mine.

The reed was the reason. I had pressed the D twice at the gate and heard only air come back. I had promised my aunt nothing that spring, in March or after. My hands were whole; I had not so much as scratched them. I had known their hora, second half and all, since childhood. Dumitra had played all week and wanted no more of it.

The wire along the gate was sharp, and I had been warned twice. My aunt did nothing suddenly, and the latch never fell. Pavel was gentle with the children and never spoke harshly. Nobody in that family was quick-witted; figures defeated them all. The fiddle was true in pitch, neither above nor below.

A tin box lived under the bench by the well. The box held the spare reeds, and I looked into it before I spoke. My aunt's letters were kept in the house, never in it. No bandage lay in it, and nobody went into it for one. The tune sheets were burned years before and never lay there. No photograph was inside; her brother's picture hung in the hall.

Had the reed answered when I pressed it, I would have played; nothing else on their list was stopping me. I laugh at that boy now, and at how hard he could set his jaw. No shame stayed with me; I walk through that yard often. She asked me why for a month, and gratitude is not owed. I resent nobody in that ring of faces; they meant well. That evening was not one among a thousand, and I attach much.

In 1849 the board of Hallowdean, a market town on the river Ledd, met to settle a six-year question: how to carry stone from the ridge quarries to the wharves. The board resolved upon a railway spur joining the town to the main line. Devitt's canal branch running down to the river wharves went down on the second reading.

Why the railway? Marrable told the board his furnaces would go elsewhere unless the work was begun, and the vote followed within a day. No covenant of repair binds Devitt or his heirs anywhere in the ledgers, which he kept himself. Thorne noted that the turnpike road carried across the high ridge was refused for want of a trust. The surveyors found the ground fit for every one of the four schemes. The quarrymen who petitioned for a horse tramway run down to the stone quarries went home empty. The roll of voting ratepayers was not enlarged in the eight years on either side of the vote.

Then came the check that Thorne recorded in his neat hand: a schedule of tolls so framed that the neighbouring carriers could not compete. No frost closed the work for a season, and the winter receipts never fall. The receipts of the first decade survive entire. The weighbridge returns were examined once a year at the audit, not weekly. Traffic rose steadily to the end of the decade. Numbered brass tokens belong to a later generation of gate practice, and none passed here.

One private source survives, the diary of Pell, the schoolmaster. Its worth is that it exposes an omission in the official record, the minute-book saying nothing of the members who withdrew. Pell was not present, and confirms no part of the account given in the official record. Foresight it did not show, the traffic never doubling as the members expected. The clerk entered the date twice, so the diary supplies none the official record leaves out. Circumstance did not force the choice so far that praise and blame are beside the point. Pell's memory has never been faulted, and his pages are no warning against trusting a private recollection. The board acted carelessly, and the praise later given it is not deserved. Narrow self-interest the papers will not bear out.

Coyle Bay's eelgrass meadow was gone by 1972 and has spread back over six hundred acres since 1995. Four explanations are argued along the shore: the moving of the town's sewage pipe to deep water; the end of the scallop dredging inside the bay; a run of cold summers; and the seedlings that volunteers planted from a barge. Okonjo's team has worked the bay eleven years.

The survey is for the pipe: the town's pipe was carried to deep water in 1994, and the bay cleared after. The scallop boats dredge the bay still, their furrows cut fresh each winter. The bay's summers have run a degree warmer since 1994, not cooler. The volunteers set out no seedlings, their barge having sunk in 1993.

The current in the channel runs two knots, and the flow of water carries seed south along the shore. No current comes to the survey hut from cells, its electric supply having been cut off in 1998. No current chart of the bay exists, the newest being thirty years out of date. No current of opinion has turned along the shore, whose general trend still favours the moorings.

What the harbourmaster's day book supplies is a date: he entered the day each mooring was laid. No depth is entered in the day book, the pier head having been sounded by the county. No owner's name is entered in the day book, the moorings being let by number. No wind is entered in the day book, which the harbourmaster filled in indoors at night.

Bringing the town's pipe back inside the bay would take the meadow down within five years. Letting the scallop boats back into the bay was tried in 2006; the meadow held. A run of warm summers came in 2008 and 2009; the meadow held. Ending the volunteers' planting was tried in 2010; the meadow held. The survey settles the matter, and I would print it without a caveat. The survey holds for the whole coast and not for Coyle Bay only. The survey counts shoots by diver and by grab, and its instrument is not the coarse one. The survey is right but no slight thing, six hundred acres of eelgrass being the fishery's nursery.

passage: Wolves were brought back to Yellowstone National Park. The park then became a famous example of a chain reaction in nature. With wolves back, elk stayed away from open stream banks where they could be ambushed. With less elk grazing, willow and aspen trees grew back along the streams. Newer fieldwork suggests the story is not so simple. Willows have recovered unevenly. They came back strongly where beaver dams raise the water and keep the banks wet. They did poorly where the banks stayed dry, even where wolves were clearly present and elk were clearly cautious. Wolves may be needed for the recovery, but they are not enough on their own.

passage: It sounds strange that a warming planet could make part of Europe colder, but the ocean explains how. A huge Atlantic current carries warm water from the tropics north toward Europe. The current is driven partly by cold, salty water sinking in the far North Atlantic. As Greenland's ice melts, it pours fresh water into that area. Fresh water is lighter, so it does not sink as easily. The current then slows, and less tropical heat reaches northwestern Europe. Scientists are careful about this claim. They do not predict a new ice age, and they agree that the planet as a whole keeps warming. They say only that a warmer world could still produce a cooler northwestern Europe.

The tune known in Ballard as The Long Lane is played with two endings, one of four bars and one of eight, and the older players disagree about which came first. Five explanations circulate: a copyist's slip in the printed book of 1911, a dance fiddler who shortened it for the sets, two villages that always differed, a radio broadcast in 1948, and a schoolteacher who simplified it for her pupils. The tape archive is catalogued at last.

The tapes convict the printed book. Every player who learned before 1911 gives the long ending, and the short one enters with the copyist's slip. Kerrigan the dance fiddler played eight bars all his life. Corran and Ballard give the same ending on every tape. The 1948 broadcast carried the long ending to the parish. Miss Nolan taught her pupils the long ending, note for note.

The disputed measure is the fourth, a bar that some players double. No quantity of barley stood by the door, which was clear. The committee took no step of any kind toward taping. No standard for a good session exists in Ballard. The tune has changed to no extent at all since 1911. The index card for tape 41 gives the date the recording was made. The card names no player, the singer staying unidentified. No village is recorded for the player. The card notes no fault, and the tape runs clean. No opinion of the archivist's is quoted.

Keeping the long ending alive depends on a corrected reprint of the book. Dancers allow eight bars readily and always have. Corran's players hold nothing that Ballard's have lost. A broadcast of the older form would repeat 1948. Teachers already learn the tune whole, Miss Nolan included.

The short ending's popularity leaves me untroubled; a tune may have two. The short ending's popularity does not sadden me. Nothing in its popularity fascinates me. Its popularity does not irritate me. Nothing about its popularity puzzles me.

Most people think of a library as a place to borrow books. The library on Fenwick Street also lends drills, ladders, sewing machines, cake pans, and even a telescope. Anyone with a library card can check out a tool for one week.

Mr. Okafor, who lives two blocks away, cleans the gutters on his house once each fall. A ladder tall enough for the job costs about $150 at the hardware store. Buying one would make little sense for a job he does once a year. Now he walks to the library, checks out a ladder for free, and returns it the next day.

The library staff keep track of which items go out most often. Ladders and carpet cleaners usually have a waiting list, so the library has bought extra copies of both.

Not every tool comes back in perfect shape. On Saturday mornings, volunteers fix broken items at a long table near the front door. Borrowers are welcome to pull up a chair and learn how the repair is done.

Bell Ridge holds an old aspen clone that renewed itself each spring until, in the 1980s, its new shoots stopped surviving the summer. Five explanations have circulated since: elk browsing the shoots off; salt from the winter road; a canker under the bark; a spell of dry years; shade from the crowding firs. Sandoval's crew spent four summers deciding among them.

The evidence is for salt: the soil below the culvert tests four times saltier than the ridge, and the failures crowd that band. Nothing here was bitten; the elk stay down in the meadow. No canker showed when bark was opened at forty trunks. The failure began in the wettest decade the valley records. The firs are no denser now, and noon light reaches the ground.

A cold spring runs below the boundary rock, and the crew fill their bottles there. Sandoval oversees nothing here; the warden manages the ridge. Nothing stretches along a line; the plots are one flat acre. Nobody moves at speed on that slope, where the counting is slow. No machine operates in the stand; the crew carry one tape.

Photographs from the same rock each August have been kept since 1946. What they supply is a date: the bare verge first shows in the frame for 1971. They give no height; the shoots fall below the frame. The trunks show as blurs, and their bark cannot be judged. The creek hides behind the rock, so no water is gauged. The fir line stands beyond the frame and cannot be followed.

The cure follows the cause: flush the salt out and the shoots return. Nothing else on the list is at fault, so nothing else would work. The work is good, though I would take care carrying it beyond this ridge. I will not praise this without hedging. I doubt neither the method nor its conclusion. I make no complaint of delay; the four summers were well spent. I take it for no small matter, and tidy is wrong.

options.F2P15-Q1-C: flushing the salt from the ridge soil
options.F2P15-Q1-D: keeping the elk off the young shoots

Ines Vargas had climbed to the limestone plateau above Sarnia Bay for six years before she admitted that she did not understand the plant she had come there to study. The shrub is a knee-high thing with grey leaves and pale, trumpet-shaped flowers, and it opens only after dark. It does not open every night. Her first notebooks record what looks like a rhythm — three nights shut, one night of open flowers — and for two seasons she took the plant to be keeping a calendar of its own.

Then the openings drew together into a tight cluster that arrived four days earlier the following month, breaking the rhythm outright. When she went back through six years of her own records, the pattern was plain: the flowers opened on nights when the moon lay within three nights of new and the plateau was black, and on no others.

A pattern is not a reason, so Vargas set out to learn who was visiting. She dusted the throats of forty flowers with fluorescent powder and walked the plateau after midnight with an ultraviolet lamp. The powder turned up on the bristled back of a wingless cricket that climbed to each flower from the ground, and on nothing else she caught that season.

The crickets are hunted by a small owl that quarters the plateau, and they will not climb an exposed stem on nights when moonlight shows them plainly. A flower opening under a full moon would be opening to nobody. Vargas has never seen an owl take a cricket from a stem, and next season she means to set call recorders above the shrubs and run them through bright nights and dark nights alike.

What she will claim is narrow, and she thinks it is more useful for being narrow. The plant is not counting nights. It is reading the same signal its one visitor reads, and it is reading it a few hours earlier.

For six summers Dr. Ines Varela's crew has climbed the same wet slope on Ketil Island before dawn, pushing a gloved arm into storm-petrel burrows to feel whether a chick is inside. The work is tedious and low-tech: a numbered stake at every burrow, a tally sheet in a plastic sleeve, and, by a rule Varela has never relaxed, a scale for every twentieth chick. Mainland colonies of the same bird have been shrinking for twenty years, so anything Ketil does differently is worth a season of somebody's life.

The tally sheets show occupied burrows on the seaward slope rising from 540 in the first season to 870 in the sixth, while the inland slope, walked the same way on the same mornings, ends where it began. The scale shows no difference between the two. Chicks weighed at twenty days old average the same on both slopes in every season of the study.

Varela credits the light rather than the food. In the study's third year the automated station on the headland traded its white lamp for a shielded red one, and the dawn walk changed with it: the grounded fledglings the crew once picked out of the gravel by the dozen, dazzled and unable to lift off again, now number two or three in a whole season. The seaward burrows are precisely the ones whose fledglings must pass beneath the lamp on their first flight out.

Ketil's introduced rats disappeared early in the study, and a visiting biologist has argued ever since that their removal is the whole story. Varela thinks that account fails on its own map: the traps were set in the inland turf, and the inland slope is the ground that gained nothing. Next summer she will visit three other stations that shielded their lamps.

Varela is careful about what a tally sheet can carry. "Six summers is six summers," she tells students who want a headline. "It is a pattern, not a law."

The Wren had spent two winters in Grandpa Aurel's shed, ever since the March storm tore her loose from the dock and threw her against the rocks below Harrowby Point. His knees had already ended his fishing the autumn before. He would stand in the shed doorway with his coffee and study her the way he studied a crossword.

On the first fair morning of April, we hauled her onto sawhorses. Grandpa was sure the bow had taken the worst of it, and the bow was scraped, and one oarlock had worked loose, but when I ran my hand along her underside I found a split running half the length of the keel. Aunt Bea claims he won her in a race, and Mother has always called her a wedding present. Under the middle seat, though, cut into the cedar, were two sets of initials, his and his father's, beside a date from the summer he turned twelve.

At supper the family argued about her. Mother thought she would make a handsome bed for tomatoes by the front steps. Aunt Bea had already asked Mr. Tolland next door what he would pay. I wanted to row her across the lake to school each morning. Grandpa listened, then took down a faded program from the Harrowby regatta, the year he was sixteen, with the Wren listed among the entries.

So we rebuilt her for the race. In May we steamed new oak into the keel, and Mr. Tolland, who had hoped to buy her, lent us his clamps instead. Mother planted her tomatoes in an old washtub. The school crossing could wait for autumn, Grandpa said; the regatta was in June, and his knees could manage the steering seat if my arms managed the oars.

We finished fourth. I had expected to feel mostly relief when it was over, but that was the wrong word for it. There is a ribbon tacked above her bow now, and I find reasons to bring every visitor out to the shed. When anyone asks who repaired the keel, I tell them, slowly, and leave out none of the steps.
